newsitem.title: FRANCE: JOBS-Minimum wage in Europe looks set to stay.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-Minimum wage in Europe looks set to stay.

text.p: European economies may be crippled by the highest levels of unemployment since World War II and calls for structural reform may persist, but one measure -- the minimum wage -- looks set to stay.

Even in Britain, where the ruling Conservatives fete a flexible labour market as the key to reducing unemployment to a six-year low, an increasingly business-friendly opposition Labour Party has stuck to its commitment to introducing a minimum wage if it takes power in elections this year.

In the rest of the European Union, politicians show no signs of sidelining policies designed to ensure minimum standards for workers, and are likely to push for greater harmonisation as countries move towards monetary union in 1999.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker told a business lunch last week the EU would have to look at anomalies in social and labour conditions. "We have to have a foundation of minimum social rights," he said.

Former British prime minister Edward Heath enlivened the pre-election debate about the minimum wage last month saying it was a valuable tool in preventing exploitation of workers if set at the right level.

In the United States, held up as the model of a flexible free-market economy, the ruling Democrats pushed through an increase in the minimum wage last year which had fallen close to a 40-year low in inflation-adjusted terms.

Robert Reich, the outgoing U.S. Labour Secretary, argued that his push for a higher minimum wage was driven by a "moral obligation". He said most Americans were willing to allow free market forces to decide but there were exceptions where society insisted on imposing minimum standards.
RECENT STUDIES CUT BOTH WAYS
And in what has always been a sensitive debate, a series of recent studies have ensured the free-market wisdom that a minimum wage cuts jobs can no longer be taken for granted.

"A priori if you say the minimum wage is a bad thing you can find studies that support your view. If you think the opposite you can find studies which will muddy the water," Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident, said.

The free-market argument against the minimum wage is that labour markets are structured so wages accurately reflect the value of goods produced. Any attempt to set wages above market levels would result in firms cutting jobs to maintain profits.

But economists in the other camp argue that inefficiences in labour markets allow employers to pay workers less than the value of what they produce so a minimum wage would not necessarily lead to jobs being cut.

An influential study published in 1994 by Princeton professors David Card and Alan Krueger showed a 19 percent rise in the minimum wage in New Jersey had no negative impact on employment at fast food restaurants.
It showed employment rose by more than in neighbouring Pennsylvania where the minimum wage remained unchanged. Other academics have questioned their findings.

In another survey of the British labour market, Amanda Gosling at the London-based Institute of Fiscal Studies said four recent studies showed a minimum wage set at the right level would not adversely affect employment.

Most economists agree that a minimum wage set too high would lead to a loss of jobs, as the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) has said was the case in France in the late 1970s and 80s.

Julian Morgan, economist at the National Institute for Economic and Social Research in London said, "It does matter very much which rate the minimum wage is set at, but a low rate may not be that damaging."
He said what is important is to work out why wages in any particular industry are low. If they are low because of competition from developing countries a minimum wage could be detrimental.

But in service industries, for example, employers can often set wages below the level they can afford to pay, he said. "I think there is a lot to be said for a sector-specific minimum wage," Morgan said.

Other economists argue that a minimum wage should take into consideration the type of person on such salaries. Young workers looking for experience, living at home, would not need to be paid as much as an unskilled 40-year old with four children doing a similar job, they say.
In its 1994 jobs study, the OECD said minimum wages should be graded by age, as in the Netherlands where each annual age group from 15 to 22 has a specific minimum wage.
The minimum wage debate appears to have shifted to how it should be set rather than whether it should exist.
DEBATE SET TO INTENSIFY?

It also looks likely to intensify after the switch to monetary union, when jobs will remain a key economic variable. Currencies and interest rates will be merged, and fiscal policy tightly constrained by an agreement to limit budget deficits.

But while some economists and officials want to focus on how to set an appropriate minimum wage to allow Europe to compete, for others the issues are inextricably linked with preserving social standards.

Stefan Stern at the British Industrial Society, an independent training and advisory body funded by public and private sector businesses and organisations, said efforts to compete with low-wage developing countries would be short-sighted.
"What sort of jobs do we want to have? Is that a game we can win in the long-run anyway?" he said.
